analysis.one_liner: Lets merchants route credit card payments over competing networks to cut swipe fees.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved since it was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on January 13, 2026, with 8 cosponsors split evenly between Democrats and Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Federal Reserve to write rules so that credit cards issued by banks with over $100 billion in assets can be processed over at least two competing payment networks, not just Visa or Mastercard. It bars banks and networks from restricting routing, penalizing merchants for choosing a cheaper network, or locking in security technology that rivals cannot use. The goal is to give merchants a choice among networks so interchange fees, the 'swipe fees' merchants pay on every credit card sale, face real competition.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants, from large retailers to small businesses, gain the ability to route credit transactions over any network that can process them, which would let them shop for lower processing fees. Consumers benefit indirectly: if interchange costs fall, merchants have room to hold prices down, though the bill does not require them to pass savings along. Larger card-issuing banks and the Visa and Mastercard networks bear the cost, since competition directly attacks the fees they collect on every transaction.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Reserve to write rules barring large card issuers from restricting a credit card to a single network, or to two networks under common control, effectively forcing at least two unaffiliated routing options on covered cards.

Prohibits card issuers and networks from inhibiting a merchant's right to direct how a credit transaction is routed, from requiring exclusive security technology that rival networks cannot use, or from penalizing a merchant for choosing a cheaper network.
Covers transactions where the card is not physically presented, including online and mobile-app purchases, so the routing choice applies to e-commerce as well as in-store sales.

Directs the Federal Reserve and Treasury to publish a list of card networks deemed national security risks or owned by foreign state entities, excluding them from the routing choices banks can mandate.

analysis.who_pays: The largest card-issuing banks (those with more than $100 billion in assets) and the dominant card networks, chiefly Visa and Mastercard, would face competition on the routing fees banks and networks collect per transaction. Cardholders could see rewards programs trimmed if issuers lose interchange revenue, and network-owned cards like American Express and Discover are untouched because the bill exempts three-party systems entirely.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts three-party systems, meaning cards where the issuer is the network or under common ownership with it, such as American Express and Discover, are entirely outside the rules, and it applies only to issuers with more than $100 billion in assets.
The bill strips the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau of any authority to enforce its requirements, leaving enforcement to Federal Reserve regulations alone.

Nothing in the bill requires merchants to pass any fee savings to customers; the mechanism, as with the 2010 debit card routing rules, lowers merchants' costs, but whether shoppers see lower prices depends on competition among retailers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and follows a tested precedent: the 2010 debit-card routing mandate gave merchants routing choice and measurably cut debit interchange, while banks responded with higher account fees and some rewards cuts. The same dynamic could apply here, with merchants the clearest winners and cardholders exposed to reduced rewards if issuers lose swipe-fee revenue. The bill's carve-outs (three-party networks, all banks under $100 billion) narrow the fight to the very top of the market, and moving enforcement out of the CFPB weakens oversight of whatever rules the Fed writes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 13, 2026 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lance Gooden (R-TX) introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2026 in the House on January 13, 2026, introducing it together with Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA).
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, which is the only action it has received.
Eight House members have cosponsored the bill, four Democrats and four Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to take a position beyond sponsorship: the dominant card networks and the largest card-issuing banks keep the current routing arrangements and interchange revenue intact for as long as the bill sits without committee action, as earlier versions of this same proposal did in previous Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Card networks and big banks, so far

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Democratic co-sponsor.

for.name: 4 of 217 House Democrats and 4 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, splitting evenly between the parties.

for.name: Retail and merchant trade groups
for.what_they_did: Have publicly promoted versions of this routing-competition bill in Congress as a way to cut merchants' swipe fees.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 13, 2026 and has taken no further action on it.

against.name: Card networks and large card-issuing banks
against.what_they_did: Have lobbied against versions of this proposal in prior Congresses, arguing routing mandates would not lower prices for consumers and would fund card rewards with less reliability.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is evenly split, with a Republican lead sponsor, a Democratic co-introducer, and cosponsorship from four Democrats and four Republicans; no member has opposed it on the record.

industries.note: The bill's central purpose is to end the networks' control over how credit transactions are routed, which is the foundation of the interchange fees merchants pay on every sale. The two largest networks are explicitly the target: the bill's rules bar covered cards from being restricted to the two biggest networks alone.

industries.industry: Large card-issuing banks (over $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: These banks collect a share of interchange on every credit transaction and issue the cards the bill covers; routing competition would squeeze that revenue. All smaller issuers are exempt under the $100 billion threshold.

Merchants would gain the right to route transactions over any qualifying network and shop for lower processing costs, savings that can flow to consumers as lower prices if retail competition forces it.
Three-party systems, where the issuer is the network or under common ownership with it, are expressly exempt from the bill, leaving their closed-loop model untouched.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress is in session, but the bill has sat untouched in the Financial Services Committee since referral. Similar credit-card routing bills attracted far larger bipartisan coalitions in earlier Congresses and still never reached a floor vote, so the realistic path is continued inaction unless the provision is attached to broader legislation moving through committee.
